clue.text: Ones who do sums to slice when wastage occurs, finding turning point

parts.note: people who sum things up, read literally as sum-mers

indicators.note: wastage means wear and damage, so the letters get knocked out of their original order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Accountants are told to cut costs wherever money is being wasted, and they find a turning point.
explanation.walkthrough: The break between the pieces falls one letter off the enumeration: SUMMERS takes the S that begins SOLSTICE.
explanation.definitionFit: The solstice is the day the sun stops climbing and starts back, so the summer one is a literal astronomical turning point.

clue.text: Southern European Roman resort?

parts.note: S is the compass abbreviation for south

indicators.note: read as re-sort, to sort again, so the letters are put into a fresh order

parts.note: E is the standard abbreviation for European
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about whether some Italian holiday spot counts as a southern European resort.
explanation.walkthrough: The last word works twice: as the definition and, split as re-sort, as the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: San Remo is a well-known seaside town on the Italian Riviera, famous as a holiday destination and for its casino.

clue.text: Craze that is, we're told, increasingly 'leonine'?

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a lion is leonine because it has a mane, so more leonine is more maney

explanation.surface: Someone describes a fad that is getting ever more lion-like.
explanation.walkthrough: Leonine is a joke synonym for having a mane; the comparative 'manier' is said the same as MANIA in non-rhotic British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A mania is a passing enthusiasm gripping many people at once, which is exactly what a craze is.

clue.text: In East End that man's going to relent

indicators.note: London's East End means Cockney speech, which drops the opening H and is reproduced by its sound

parts.note: he's off means he is leaving, and a Cockney drops the H

explanation.surface: In London's East End someone announces that a man is about to give way.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney, the accent of London's East End, drops the H, so 'he's off' comes out as 'e's off.
explanation.definitionFit: To relent is to soften or slacken in severity, and to ease off is the idiom for lessening pressure.

clue.text: At first surgeon dresses … wrapping key component of cleaning wounds

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the next word only

parts.note: opening letter of the word

indicators.note: to wrap something is to go all round it, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: A-lines are dresses flaring from a fitted top
a key is the set of answers, or a means of solving

explanation.surface: A surgeon first dresses a wound, wrapping it, with the key part of cleaning it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dresses' tempts as the verb for bandaging a wound, but it is the noun: a style of frock named for its shape like a capital A.
explanation.definitionFit: Salt-water solutions are the standard sterile liquid used to rinse and irrigate wounds before dressing them.

clue.text: Librarian and rhymester, Kingston-upon-Hull's ill-humoured notable, primarily?

definitions.text: Librarian and rhymester, Kingston-upon-Hull's ill-humoured notable, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives only its leading letter

parts.words: Librarian and rhymester, Kingston-upon-Hull's ill-humoured notable
parts.note: the heads of the six words

explanation.surface: A potted biography of a grumpy poet who ran a university library in Hull.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both describes the man and, by its initials, spells his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Philip Larkin, the famously gloomy poet, worked for decades as librarian of the University of Hull.

clue.text: Isaac's son devoured by songbird, detailed in book

indicators.note: what is devoured ends up inside the eater, so one piece sits within another
read as de-tailed, with its tail cut off, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a familiar singing bird
Esau, twin of Jacob, was the son of Isaac in Genesis

explanation.surface: A biblical figure is eaten by a bird, as recorded in some book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like 'described closely' but splits as de-tailed, so the bird loses its last letter before it does any eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A thesaurus is a reference volume of synonyms, so it is a kind of book.

clue.text: Being a little economical, I costed plain white fabrics

indicators.note: only a small part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A thrifty shopper prices up some cheap white cloth.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts in the tail of 'economical' and ends at the start of 'costed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Calico is an inexpensive unbleached cotton cloth, so several kinds of it are plain white textiles.

clue.text: A refusal in Paris will be coming soon

parts.note: taken as written
French for no

explanation.surface: Someone in Paris says no, but promises it will happen shortly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Paris' signals a French word, as cities often do in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Anon is an old-fashioned adverb meaning shortly or presently, so something anon is on its way soon.

clue.text: These are collarless, fitted and they might keep you warm

indicators.note: something fitted has been shaped and adjusted, so the letters are reworked into new form

parts.note: taken as written, ready to rearrange

explanation.surface: It sounds like a description of neckless, tailored shirts that keep the wearer warm.
explanation.walkthrough: The clothing picture is misleading: 'fitted' also fits panels fitted to a roof.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar panels generate power that can run home heating, so they are a loose, playful way of being kept warm.

clue.text: Gelato blended smoothly

indicators.note: blending mixes things together, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Italian ice cream has been whizzed in a blender until silky.
explanation.walkthrough: Both the fodder and the result are Italian, which helps the surface hang together.
explanation.definitionFit: Legato is the musical direction to play notes connected without breaks, an adverb for flowing performance.

clue.text: Endless, unceasing, awful pest

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped
something awful is in a terrible state, so the letters are mangled

parts.note: the word minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone complains about a pest that never stops bothering them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' and 'unceasing' look like a pair of near-synonyms piled up for effect; the first is an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A pest is an annoying person or thing, and a nuisance is the common word for such an irritant.

clue.text: 'Slow down!' making you more likely to run?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a command to stop and think

definitions.text: making you more likely to run
definitions.note: a description of a dye rather than a phrase meaning the same
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a colour that is less colourfast bleeds in the wash

explanation.surface: Someone is told to slow down, as if going slower made them likelier to bolt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' looks like moving at speed; it is what dye does in the wash when it is not fast.
explanation.definitionFit: Fast dyes hold their colour; a less fast one bleeds, while the phrase is also an idiomatic warning to wait.

clue.text: The writer supports peaceful … engrossing … good time in national park

indicators.note: in a down clue a support sits underneath, so this piece goes at the bottom
to engross is to absorb fully, so one piece takes another inside it

parts.note: calm and untroubled
G is the abbreviation for good
T is the abbreviation for time
the setter refers to themself

explanation.surface: A writer endorses a calm, absorbing holiday in a national park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter, I; in a down entry it supports the rest by sitting at the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The Serengeti in Tanzania is one of Africa's most famous national parks, known for its great wildebeest migration.

clue.text: Berries regularly consumed in Jewish rite

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: Fruit is eaten as part of a Jewish ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consumed in' looks like a container signal but here only joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The bris, or brit milah, is the Jewish circumcision ceremony held for a baby boy on his eighth day.

clue.text: Goddess of discord returns to see father

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way one came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: Eris is the Greek goddess of strife

explanation.surface: A troublemaking goddess comes home to visit her dad.
explanation.walkthrough: Eris threw the golden apple that started the Trojan War, hence goddess of discord.
explanation.definitionFit: To sire is to beget offspring, and as a noun a sire is a male parent, especially of an animal.

clue.text: In Jacques Tati's 'Trafic' we see advocate of big government

indicators.note: inside the following words, so the letters are found within them

parts.note: the letters straddle the three words

explanation.surface: Watching the French comedy film Trafic, someone spots a political message about the state.
explanation.walkthrough: Jacques Tati was a French comic filmmaker; Trafic (1971) is his car-show comedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Statism is the belief that the state should control much of economic and social life, so a statist favours large government.

clue.text: Boycotts sick-looking film about ballet

parts.note: to black a firm or goods is to boycott them, in trade-union usage
pale and unwell

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to watch an unhealthy-looking dance movie.
explanation.walkthrough: To black something is chiefly British trade-union slang for refusing to handle it; the pieces split one letter away from the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Swan is the 2010 Darren Aronofsky psychological thriller about a ballerina dancing Swan Lake.

clue.text: Noisy beasts, 101 reprobates, Australian being hugged

parts.note: CI is 101 in Roman numerals

indicators.note: what is hugged is held within arms, so it sits inside another piece

parts.note: cads are dishonourable men
A is a standard abbreviation for Australian

explanation.surface: Like a hundred and one Dalmatians, a gang of rowdy rogues are embracing an Australian.
explanation.walkthrough: The number is Roman numerals; the rogues wrap the Aussie.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicadas are insects whose males make a loud, shrill buzz, making them famously loud creatures.

clue.text: On the radio a contender's coming

indicators.note: radio is heard not seen, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

parts.note: a contender is a competitor

explanation.surface: A radio announcer says a challenger is on the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A coming, as a noun, is the act of getting to a place, which is what an arrival is.

clue.text: Drink raised taking note of a king

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something up makes it read bottom to top
to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside

parts.note: a type of beer
N is the dictionary abbreviation for note

explanation.surface: Someone raises a glass to toast a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' looks like the toast but reverses the beer upward in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Regnal means relating to a reign or monarch, as in regnal years counted from a sovereign's accession.

clue.text: Superlatively skilful, refined ancients

indicators.note: refining reprocesses material into a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A tribute to the most accomplished and cultured of the old civilisations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refined' reads as cultured, describing the ancients, but it signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Canny means shrewd and clever, so its superlative describes the most adept and astute.

clue.text: Socialist actors run out

parts.note: the actors in a production
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
O is a standard abbreviation for out

explanation.surface: Left-wing actors leave the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run out' looks like one phrase, a cricket dismissal, but gives two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Fidel Castro led Cuba's communist revolution, so he is a famous example of a socialist leader.

clue.text: What you're trying to do, alone, very engrossed

indicators.note: something engrossed is wholly absorbed, so it sits inside another piece

parts.note: single, by oneself
V is the abbreviation for very

explanation.surface: A description of the solver at work, alone and deeply absorbed.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks to the reader directly: right now you are trying to work out this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The crossword reader's aim is to work out each clue, so the setter describes the reader's own task.

clue.text: With feet pointing inward, glutton takes age to come forward at last

parts.note: a greedy eater
a vast period of time
taken as written

indicators.note: at the end, so only the final letter of each word is kept

parts.note: the tail letters of the two words

explanation.surface: A greedy, knock-kneed eater takes ages before finally stepping up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come forward' reads as a phrase but supplies just its two final letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigeon-toed describes a gait in which the toes turn in towards each other, as in a walking pigeon.

clue.text: Ultimately frugal: Everyman has to be

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: final letter of the word
the setter, Everyman, says I have, contracted to I've

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to having to be thrifty in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has to' looks like obligation; it splits, with 'to' just a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in the sense of to exist is to have life, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Listen: eat less, starting with small cutlery?

indicators.note: starting with tells us what comes first in the answer, ahead of everything else

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small
taken as written, letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A diet tip: cut down, beginning with smaller knives and forks.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no anagram signal; the question mark admits the liberty. The definition is by example, since much cutlery is made of this metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Most knives, forks and spoons are made from this rust-resistant alloy, so the metal stands for table utensils.
